vignette:
Kareem, a 54-year-old Middle Eastern American community organizer, came to treatment after years of trying to keep himself moving through work, family life, and public meetings while never quite feeling safe in his own skin. The assault that changed him had happened in the apartment he shared with his then partner, a man he had trusted completely. What began as an argument in a dark hallway escalated into physical abuse that left Kareem pinned, frightened, and unable to make sense of where one moment ended and the next began. Even now, his memories of that night returned in disconnected pieces: the smell of the apartment, a hand grabbing his arm, the pounding in his ears, the flash of a wall, and, most intrusively, fragments of sounds he had heard during the attack. When he was overtaken by those memories, he sometimes heard those same sounds in his head as if they were happening again, and the recollection could be brought on instantly by something in his surroundings without warning. A dim corridor, a shadowed stairwell, or the sound of a helicopter or low-flying aircraft over the neighborhood could pull him back before he had time to prepare.

From the beginning, Kareem made sense of the event through a painful set of conclusions about himself and other people. He said he had been betrayed by someone he trusted, and that betrayal seemed to confirm for him that the world no longer worked the way he had believed it did. He spoke with shame about the thought that the abuse happened because of the sort of person he was, as if there were something about him that invited mistreatment. Those beliefs did not stay abstract; they colored the memories themselves. When an image of the attack surfaced, it came attached to self-condemnation and to the conviction that trust was foolish, so the memory felt not only vivid but morally loaded, as if each fragment proved that he had misjudged both his partner and himself. Over time, the same remembered pieces deepened his sense that everything he once relied on had been destroyed.

Kareem's attempts to cope slowly hardened into habits that shaped his days. He became vigilant for dangerous people, scanning faces in crowds, watching hands, and checking exits whenever he entered a meeting hall, parking garage, or public building. He avoided the site where the assault had taken place, taking longer routes home and declining invitations that would bring him near that street. He also began wearing concealing clothing, favoring loose layers and darker jackets that helped him feel less visible, as though being harder to notice might keep him from becoming a target again. These strategies briefly lowered his alarm, but they also kept his fear alive. Because he was constantly watching for threat, ordinary movement in a doorway, a stranger standing too close, or a sudden shadow in a hallway became more likely to catch his attention, and each new jolt could unexpectedly call up the old memory. In that way, the very effort to protect himself made the world feel full of possible dangers and made his trigger list grow broader.

The more often the memories broke through, the more Kareem returned to the same explanations. Each intruding fragment seemed to confirm that he was marked by what had happened, that he had failed to read the danger correctly, and that the world could no longer be trusted. Those appraisals intensified his sense of threat, and his scanning became more relentless. At work, in his role as a community organizer, he found himself preoccupied with who might be unsafe in the room, while the dark basement meeting spaces and windowless offices he sometimes had to use became especially hard to tolerate. He began arriving early to choose seats, leaving before others, and turning down evening events that would have kept him out after sunset. The concealing clothing and avoidance of the old site protected him from brief spikes of panic, but they also narrowed his life and reinforced the belief that danger was everywhere and that he himself was somehow the reason it had found him.

By the time Kareem sought help, he was exhausted by the loop of being set off, reliving the assault in fragments and sounds, and then retreating further into suspicion and self-blame. He feared that one unguarded moment in the dark, one unexpected aircraft overhead, or one accidental return to that neighborhood could bring the whole memory crashing back again. What brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep organizing for his community while living as if every room might contain harm, and what he most hoped for was to stop feeling betrayed by the world and by himself long enough to trust his own life again.
